# OneApp (also known as "One App")

> OneApp — every tool in one place. Sketch notes, a full PDF editor, image studio, todos, reminders, timer and more. A single free offline-first (PWA) web workspace at https://oneappready.vercel.app; all data stays local in the browser, no sign-up.

## Apps

- [Sketch Notes](/): freehand drawing and note canvas
- [PDF Editor](/pdfeditor): view, edit, annotate and organize PDFs
- [Image Studio](/image): image editing and adjustments
- [Board](/board): a personal page the user composes **by prompting**. One text field takes plain-English instructions and a local, deterministic parser (no network, no API key, no model) turns each one into a single board edit. Five section types — **Note** (free text), **Checklist** (tickable rows), **Counter** (a tally with an optional goal, step and unit), **Links** (saved `http(s)` addresses) and **Habit** (a seven-day local-calendar streak). The grammar covers add ("add a checklist for groceries", "add a counter for water with a goal of 8", "add a note called Ideas"), modify ("rename groceries to shopping", "set the water goal to 10", "set the water unit to glasses", "turn ideas into a checklist", "make ideas wide", "move groceries to top", "collapse ideas"), fill in ("add milk to groceries", "add docs example.com to work", "check milk", "add 5 to water", "check today on reading") and remove ("remove milk from groceries", "remove groceries", "reset water", "clear the board", "undo"). References resolve by title, then loosely, then by type name, and an ambiguous or unknown reference is answered with which sections exist rather than a silent no-op; every phrasing is published in an in-app "What you can say" sheet whose lines are tappable and live. Every command has an equivalent direct control on the card (add-type bar, inline title editing, +/−, tick, move, width, reset, remove, change type), so the app is fully usable without composing a sentence. Undo covers the last 25 changes for the session. Fully offline; the board is stored in this browser under `sknotes:board` and never uploaded
- [Todos](/todos): task and week planner
- [Reminders](/reminders): scheduled reminders with notifications
- [Timer](/timer): pomodoro and countdown timer
- [System Info](/system): live device and system dashboard — OS, processor, memory, graphics, display, battery, network, storage, locale and the browser capability matrix, as live meters plus an exportable report. Carries a compact nearby-devices panel; the full scanner is its own app, below
- [Nearby Devices](/nearby): find the hardware around this machine and read what each piece of it is. Discovery uses every route the web platform allows — devices this site was already granted over **Web Bluetooth, WebUSB, WebHID and Web Serial**, attached microphones, speakers and cameras, connected game controllers, cast-capable displays on the local network via the Presentation API, and (on Chrome with experimental web features enabled) a **live BLE advertisement scan** streaming every broadcast in range with its signal strength. A page cannot sweep the airwaves by itself: each transport button opens the *browser's own* chooser, and only the device the user picks becomes visible to the app — attached audio, video and controller hardware needs no prompt. Selecting a device opens its full sheet, read from the descriptor the platform already returned, with no device opened, claimed or written to: **USB** — manufacturer, product, vendor/product ids, device class/subclass/protocol translated to names, USB and device revisions, and every configuration with its interfaces, alternates and endpoints (direction, transfer type, packet size); **HID** — vendor/product ids, the collection tree with usage pages and usages named, and the input/output/feature report layout; **serial** — USB vendor/product ids behind the port; **cameras and microphones** — the track capabilities the hardware advertises (resolutions, frame rates, facing mode, sample rate, channels, echo cancellation and the rest) once the site holds camera/mic permission; **controllers** — layout plus a live view of every button pressure and stick axis, which doubles as a gamepad tester. **Bluetooth** features need a live link, so a per-device "Connect & read features" action walks the GATT table — every primary service and characteristic with what it permits, plus manufacturer name, model number, firmware/hardware/software revision, appearance, transmit power and battery level — then disconnects again. A browser-support matrix shows which of the eight discovery APIs exist here, and the whole inventory copies out as a plain-text report. Fully offline (the APIs are local); everything is read on-device and nothing is transmitted
- [Speed Test](/speedtest): network speed measurement
- [News](/news): latest headlines by category — tech, software engineering, sports, national, international, state (Kerala) and local
- [World Clock](/worldclock): live time anywhere in the world, and the country behind each clock. Three views over one selection. **Clocks** — your own time leads a board of pinned cities (120+ cities across 68 countries and every inhabited time zone, including half- and quarter-hour offsets like India's UTC+05:30 and Nepal's UTC+05:45); each card shows the live time, the zone abbreviation, the offset relative to you, a "Tomorrow"/"Yesterday" badge whenever the date differs, a day/night glyph and a plain-language read on whether it is a reasonable hour to call. A time-shift slider moves every clock together by up to ±12 hours for planning a call or meeting across zones. Cities are searchable by name, former name, country, capital, ISO code or IANA zone ("bombay", "kerala", "GB", "asia/kolkata" all work) and the pinned board persists on the device. **Country** — capital, region, population (approximate, with density), area, currency and symbol, official languages, international dialling code, which side of the road it drives on, internet TLD and current UTC offset, plus a short profile and what the country is known for (its specialities), and the live local time in each of its cities. **News** — latest headlines from that country's own news edition in English. Time zones are computed with the browser's `Intl` API, so daylight saving always follows the platform's current tz database; the clocks, country details and specialities are all bundled and work fully offline, and only the headlines need a connection
- [Malayalam Writer](/malayalam): write Malayalam by transliteration (Manglish), an on-screen keyboard, or handwriting
- [Translate](/translate): translate text between languages, online (auto-detects the source) or fully offline on-device via the browser's built-in AI — no text leaves the device
- [Morse Code](/morse): learn, practise and send International Morse code. Four tools — a tappable chart of every letter, number, punctuation mark and prosign; a four-choice drill that weights unseen and shaky characters and tracks per-character mastery; a text ⇄ Morse translator that plays the message; and a straight key you hold to send, decoded live from your own timing. Speed (5–30 WPM) and sidetone pitch are adjustable, and every signal plays as sound, an on-screen lamp and optional vibration. Fully offline — the tone is synthesized with the Web Audio API, so no audio files are downloaded
- [Sound Meter](/soundmeter): measure sound from the microphone. Four readings from one live analysis — the fundamental frequency in Hz (autocorrelation, 50 Hz–2 kHz) alongside the loudest tone present; the nearest musical note with its cents error, making it a working instrument tuner (reference A adjustable 415–444 Hz); loudness as RMS and peak dBFS with a session peak hold, a clipping warning and an adjustable — explicitly uncalibrated — dB SPL estimate; and a live visualization that switches between a 20 Hz–20 kHz log-scale FFT spectrum (pointing at a peak reads out its frequency and note) and a time-domain waveform scope. Fully offline via the Web Audio API. Requires microphone permission; no audio is recorded, stored or transmitted, each frame is analysed and discarded, and the microphone is released on stopping or switching apps
- [Color Lens](/color): identify any colour in a picture. Attach an image, drop or paste one, or take a photo with the device camera (in-app viewfinder with front/rear switching, falling back to the system camera app), then tap, drag or arrow-key anywhere on it; a pixel-level loupe magnifies the sample point and the sample size is switchable between 1 px, 3×3 and 5×5 averaging. Every reading is reported in full — HEX (with the short form), RGB, HSL, HSB/HSV, CMYK, CIE L*a*b*, LCH, XYZ and WCAG relative luminance — alongside the nearest of the 148 CSS colour names (matched by ΔE in L*a*b*), perceived brightness, a warm/cool read, and contrast ratios against white and black graded to WCAG 2.2 AA, AA-large and AAA with live text samples. It also extracts the image's dominant palette by median cut (4, 6, 8 or 12 swatches, each with the share of the picture it covers) plus the overall average colour, and derives complementary, analogous, triadic, split-complementary, tetradic and monochromatic schemes and a nine-step tint/shade ramp from whatever is picked. Palettes export as a hex list, CSS variables, a Tailwind v4 `@theme` block, SCSS variables or JSON. A hex code can be typed in directly instead of read from a photo, recent picks are kept on the device, and on Chromium the browser's EyeDropper API adds picking from anywhere on screen. Fully offline — the image is decoded and sampled in the browser and is never uploaded
- [Assistant](/assistant): a free in-app AI guide — ask what any app does or how to do a task, and it answers from a built-in knowledge base of the workspace and opens the right tool. It also acts on instructions typed in the chat ("open the timer", "go to PDF merge", "turn on dark mode", "open settings", "clear the chat"). No API key or account; it uses the browser's built-in on-device model when present, otherwise a bundled offline retrieval engine

## Offline / low-bandwidth behaviour

- Works 100% offline after the first visit. A service worker (/sw.js) precaches every app
  route's HTML, then stores every file in the build manifest (/precache-manifest.json) —
  which includes the code-split chunk for each of the eighteen apps. So one online visit
  to any single page is enough for every deep link (e.g. /todos, /pdfeditor) to cold-load
  with no connection, not just the app that was open when the network dropped.
- An app whose code is somehow not stored (a connection lost mid-download, or a deploy
  that renamed the chunks) shows a "not saved for offline use yet" panel with a way to
  open another app, rather than failing the whole page.
- Users can force or clear the download from Settings → Offline ("Save all apps for
  offline"). Automatic precaching is skipped on metered or 2g-class connections; the
  explicit save from Settings runs regardless.
- Offline is detected from what requests actually do, not only `navigator.onLine`, so the
  offline states also appear behind a captive portal or a dead uplink that the browser
  still reports as being online.
- On a weak connection the app serves saved content rather than stalling: navigations
  fall back to the cached shell after 3.5s, API responses after 6s.
- Fully offline: Sketch Notes, PDF Editor, Image Studio, Board, Todos, Reminders, Timer,
  System Info, Nearby Devices (the discovery APIs are local; only cast-display detection
  needs the local network), Morse Code, Sound Meter, Color Lens, Malayalam transliteration +
  keyboard, on-device Translate, Assistant, and World Clock apart from its News tab —
  clocks, time zones and every country detail are computed and bundled locally, and
  country flags fall back to the ISO code when the flag image has not been cached.
- Needs a connection: News and World Clock headlines (previously loaded headlines still
  open from cache), online
  translation (previously translated phrases still open), Malayalam handwriting
  recognition, Speed Test, public-IP lookup. Each of these states this in the UI when
  offline instead of failing silently.
- Installable as a PWA (manifest at /manifest.webmanifest, with app shortcuts).

## Settings

Opened from the bottom of the app launcher; every preference applies to all apps and is
stored on the device.

- Theme: twenty-four built-in palettes, grouped by base. Light — Light, Ocean, Sky, Mint,
  Forest, Sunset, Clay, Sand, Olive, Rose, Grape, Lavender, Slate. Dark — Dark, Midnight,
  Carbon, Abyss, Matrix, Nebula, Ember, Wine, Mocha, Arctic, Noir (Noir is pure black, for
  OLED screens). Every palette holds WCAG AA contrast on the text it carries.
  Custom themes: up to twelve of your own, each built from a base (light or dark), an
  accent and a background colour — the rest of the palette is derived from those, and the
  editor shows the accent's live contrast ratio against the background so a theme you make
  stays readable. Saved themes can be renamed, re-coloured and deleted. Everything is
  stored on the device.
- Interface: the workspace's shape, separate from its colour. Five styles — Glass
  (translucent frosted panels over an ambient wash, the default), Solid (opaque cards, no
  blur), Soft (large round corners, wide diffuse shadow), Sharp (square corners, tight
  shadow) and Outline (borders instead of shadows). Plus three densities — Compact, Cosy,
  Roomy — which scale padding, gaps and control sizes together. Style and density are
  independent, and both are stored on the device.
- Pointer: replaces the mouse cursor workspace-wide. System (the device's own) plus
  thirteen drawn presets — Arrow, Chevron, Hand, Crosshair, Dot, Ring, Pen, Pencil,
  Brush, Sparkle, Star, Heart and Pixel — each in four sizes (Small to Huge) and
  coloured by the theme, by the accent, or by a colour you pick. A pointer of your own can be made
  from any image file or emoji, rendered on the device (nothing is uploaded), with its
  hotspot at the top-left or the centre. Touch input and the drawing/text cursors are
  unaffected.
- Offline: save every app to the device, or clear what's stored.

## Notes

- No accounts, no server storage — data is kept in the browser's localStorage.
- Apps are switched from the launcher (the "Switch app" button in any app's header)
  without a page load; the URL still changes to that app's path, and the app's logo plays
  a brief opening animation over the new screen. Motion throughout the workspace is
  dropped when the browser asks for reduced motion.
- Device permissions are asked for only on the feature that needs one, and only from a
  click: notifications (Reminders), the microphone (Sound Meter) and the camera (Color
  Lens), and the per-device choosers in Nearby Devices (Bluetooth, USB, HID, serial —
  each granted one device at a time, by the browser, never by the page). Captured audio
  and video are analysed in memory and discarded — never recorded
  or transmitted — and the device is released as soon as the feature is done with it.
